title: Adams Site (15Fu4)
summary: In Fulton County, the Adams Site (15Fu4) is a Mississippian town of platform mounds and plazas, lived in from about 1100 to 1500 CE.
bodyMarkdown:
The Adams Site (15Fu4) is an ancient town in Fulton County, at the far western tip of Kentucky. The people who built it belonged to the [Mississippian](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mississippian_culture) world, the farming chiefdoms that spread across the Mississippi and Ohio valleys and much of the Southeast between about 900 and 1500 CE.

The town covers about 7.25 hectares, roughly eighteen acres. It was built on top of an older Late Woodland village, so people had already lived on this ground before the mounds went up. At its heart was a group of platform mounds set around a central plaza. A second, smaller plaza lay to the southwest of the largest mound.

Platform mounds were flat-topped earthworks. Leaders' houses, council buildings, or temples often stood on top, and the mounds were rebuilt and raised in stages over generations. The open plaza was where the town gathered for ceremonies, games, and public work.

People lived at the Adams Site from about 1100 to 1500 CE. Archaeologists divide that span into two local phases, the Medley phase (1100 to 1300) and the Jackson phase (1300 to 1500). The village refuse around the mounds, called midden, runs one to one and a half meters deep in places. That depth comes from centuries of daily life: broken pottery, food bones, ash, and house debris piling up year after year.

The farmers here grew corn, along with squash and other plants, and hunted deer and smaller game. Like other Mississippian towns, Adams was likely tied to its neighbors by trade and kinship. Other western Kentucky Mississippian places include [Sassafras Ridge](/stories/sassafras-ridge-15fu3-fulton-county/), also in Fulton County, and [Wickliffe Mounds](/stories/wickliffe-mounds-mississippian-village-ballard-county/) in Ballard County.

## Kentucky today

The Adams Site was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1984. It is not open to visitors, and its exact location is not published, to protect it from looting. The map pin is rounded to a Fulton County point. Digging into or collecting from an archaeological site or a Native grave is a crime under Kentucky law. To see a Mississippian town up close, visit Wickliffe Mounds State Historic Site.
Source: [Adams site (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adams_site)
